extracted.intended_audience: federal agency attorneys, judges, legal scholars, and policy makers concerned with First Amendment issues on government social media
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrinal and normative analysis of how First Amendment doctrines (public forum vs. government speech) apply to federal agency social media sites that invite public comment, including practical factors, categories of speech, and agency liability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the public forum doctrine or the government speech doctrine governs agency social media sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contextual, pragmatic analysis is required; courts consider context, purpose, and control. The Article argues the public forum doctrine is the appropriate framework for agency social media sites opened to public comment, because it better protects citizens' First Amendment rights and prevents arbitrary censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant Factors: Mixed Speech on Web 2.0
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech on agency social media is often a hybrid of agency speech and private speech on public issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which type of speech predominates by examining location (third-party platform vs .gov), the agency's purpose (public engagement vs conveying a government message), and the degree to which public comment dominates the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Government Speech Test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Free Speech Clause is irrelevant when the government itself is the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as government speech, the government must show it established a message and maintained effective control over the content and communication of that message. Selection of private speech is government speech only when the government acts in an institutionally specific manner (e.g., as a library, art patron, broadcaster, or university).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Public Forum Test
rubrics_metrics.description: The public forum doctrine limits government ability to restrict speech on public property and can be applied to intangible communicative realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a site is a (limited) public forum, restrictions must satisfy forum doctrine standards—limited public fora permit some permissible restrictions but protect citizen speakers' First Amendment rights; courts apply heightened scrutiny to viewpoint discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context, Pragmatism, and Supreme Court Precedent (Page, Gittens, Pleasant Grove)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts use contextual and pragmatic analysis in deciding which doctrine applies, guided by cases like Pleasant Grove City v. Summum and PETA v. Gittens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A close reading of these opinions cautions against broadly applying government speech doctrine to agency social media; consider institutional specificity and practical control in light of precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from Principle: Liberty as Non-Dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative argument that free speech entails non-dependence on the arbitrary will of others (neo‑Roman liberty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strand of republican thought supports applying the public forum doctrine to agency social media to avoid subjecting citizen speech to unaccountable discretionary government censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to Federal Agency Social Media (forum characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that open social media sites and maintain them for public comment act affirmatively to create a space functionally like public property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sites should often be characterized as limited public fora; this characterization affects permissible restrictions and the level of First Amendment protection afforded to commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location on Third-Party Platforms vs .gov Domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a site is hosted on a private third-party (.com) platform or on a .gov domain affects the state-action analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although third-party platforms are private, an agency's affirmative action in sponsoring and maintaining pages on those platforms can make them effectively public property for forum analysis. Distinguish between privately-hosted content on an agency website and agency pages on third-party services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and Use of Agency Social Media (engage the public vs convey agency message)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies pursue dual purposes: conveying information about agency activities and soliciting public input/engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the stated and practical purpose is public engagement and solicitation of comment, private speech predominates and forum analysis is favored over government-speech characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of Public Comment as a Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Many agencies actively solicit public comment on social media (Facebook, Twitter, YouTube) and sometimes direct users to agency websites for comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact of solicitation weighs in favor of treating social media pages as forums, and it impacts the permissible scope of content moderation and restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited Public Forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency social media sites are best characterized as limited public fora when opened for specific types of public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a limited public forum, the government may impose reasonable, viewpoint‑neutral restrictions but may not engage in viewpoint discrimination; evaluate restrictions under that standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-Matter Restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions that limit speech by topic or subject matter on agency social media sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject‑matter restrictions in a limited public forum may be permissible only if they are reasonable and viewpoint‑neutral; they must be evaluated in light of forum doctrine and the agency's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, Place, and Manner Restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations limiting when, where, and how speech occurs on agency social media pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such TPM restrictions must be content‑neutral, narrowly tailored to serve a significant government interest, and must leave open ample alternative channels of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility Codes and Viewpoint Neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies adopt civility codes and codes of conduct for users (often via Terms of Service) to regulate discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civility codes must be enforced in a viewpoint‑neutral manner; they cannot serve as a pretext for viewpoint discrimination. Scrutinize codes for overbroad or vague provisions that could chill protected speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unprotected Speech: Obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscenity is not protected by the First Amendment and may be restricted on agency social media sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may remove obscene content consistent with established obscenity standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unprotected Speech: Fighting Words / Incitement (Brandenburg Test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that constitutes incitement or fighting words (per Brandenburg) is not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Brandenburg incitement standard (intent, imminence, likelihood) when assessing whether speech can be restricted as unprotected incitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected Speech: Offensive, Extremist, and Profane Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive, extremist, and profane speech generally receive First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offensiveness alone is not a sufficient ground for removal; agencies must avoid removing speech solely because it is offensive or profane unless it falls into a recognized unprotected category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected Speech: Hate Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech may be offensive and harmful but is often constitutionally protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless hate speech crosses into unprotected categories (e.g., direct threats, incitement), it cannot be categorically suppressed on agency social media pages; apply forum doctrine protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful Speech: Cyberstalking and Cyberharassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech constituting cyberstalking or cyberharassment is unlawful and may be excluded or removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may restrict or remove such unlawful speech consistent with criminal statutes and constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful Speech: Defamation, Libel, and Slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamatory statements are not protected and can be subject to removal and civil liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be able to remove defamatory comments; consider libel standards and the potential need to balance removal with public-interest considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic Speech: False Statements of Fact
rubrics_metrics.description: False factual statements can be misleading and problematic in the public discourse on agency pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation of false statements of fact is sensitive; context matters and constitutional protections vary, so agencies must be cautious when removing or labeling false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Speech and Discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech and discriminatory content raise distinct issues about access and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial speech is protected under a separate doctrinal rubric (Central Hudson); discriminatory restrictions on access or participation can raise forum and equal‑protection concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability, Immunity, and Endorsement: Agency Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosting and moderating public comments may expose agencies to tort liabilities under state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess agency exposure for content hosted or removed and consider applicable immunities and risk‑management practices when setting moderation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Immunity for Constitutional Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereign immunity may limit remedies for constitutional claims against federal agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sovereign immunity doctrines when evaluating potential constitutional litigation and remedies arising from agency moderation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection or removal of third‑party speech may imply government endorsement or disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully evaluate whether agency actions amount to endorsement (which has constitutional significance) versus permissible editorial selection, especially when government acts in an institutionally specific manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Control Over Message
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of governmental control over content and communication is a key determinant in characterizing speech as governmental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the agency's practical control—technical moderation, content curation, express messaging—to determine whether the government has established and is controlling an official message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear Message Presence or Absence
rubrics_metrics.description: Government speech requires the existence of an identifiable, government‑established message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical study of agency social media sites may reveal a lack of a clear, unitary message; absence of such a message weighs against a government‑speech designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of Service and Federal-Compatible Agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often operate under third‑party Terms of Service (TOS); GSA has negotiated federal‑compatible TOS for agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TOS and negotiated agreements affect agencies' operational constraints and legal postures; review them to understand moderation rights, responsibilities, and limits when evaluating forum status and permissible restrictions.
